1: \section{Nonlinear-regime study and certificate conservatism}
2: \label{sec:transport-followup}
3: 
4: We test whether valid confidence transport produces useful certificates and
5: decisions in a controlled nonlinear model.  The prespecified follow-up evaluates
6: 600 policy trajectories; a separate 294 development and tuning trajectories
7: precede evaluation.  The original near-linear study is retained separately in
8: \Cref{sec:transport-instantiation}; its evidence is not pooled with this study.
9: 
10: \paragraph{Model and prespecified protocol.}
11: We use Gaussian observations with mean
12: $\mu_{\btheta}(z)=\sqrt W\tanh(\phi(z)^\top\btheta/\sqrt W)$,
13: with $\|\phi(z)\|_2\le1$ and projected parameters $\|\btheta\|_2\le1$.
14: Contexts have dimension four, there are five actions, and the context--action
15: feature map has dimension 29.  Noise has standard deviation $0.25$, the metric
16: ridge is one, and the confidence parameter is $\delta=0.05$.
17: A fixed teacher generates the rewards.  We fix
18: $T=1000$ and $W\in\{16,1,0.25\}$, with 50 common evaluation seeds per condition
19: and four policies.  Changing $W$ changes both the reward function and its
20: curvature; cross-condition trends do not isolate a causal effect of metric
21: drift.  The conditions were specified before their evaluation outcomes were
22: observed.  Development, tuning, and evaluation use disjoint seed sets.
23: 
24: All policies use the corrected center and confidence radius of
25: \Cref{cor:corrected-center-new}.  \emph{Hessian} uses the analytic path
26: certificate $\bar D_t^Q$; \emph{endpoint} substitutes the dense endpoint Thompson
27: distance; \emph{frozen reference} uses the reference width directly; and
28: \emph{naive current} uses the current width without transport, an uncertified
29: control.  All four policies update their representations: ``frozen'' describes
30: the collection-time metric, not a fixed representation.  They share contexts
31: and potential-noise streams but have their own adaptive action histories.
32: The common optimizer, learning rate $3\times10^{-4}$ with 20 full-batch steps
33: followed by projection each round, was selected from nine candidates by prediction MSE
34: on uniform-random tuning histories.  This controls one implementation choice;
35: it does not establish policy-specific regret-optimal tuning.
36: 
37: Dense float64 matrices and Cholesky solves implement the exact-operator
38: abstraction, and finite action enumeration uses the smallest-index tie rule.
39: This is a 29-parameter diagnostic study, not a test of approximate solvers,
40: large-model scalability, or real-data performance.  Further protocol and
41: provenance details appear in \Cref{app:transport-followup}.
42: 
43: \paragraph{Prespecified policy outcomes.}
44: Hessian transport has higher mean cumulative pseudo-regret than every
45: comparator in every condition (\Cref{fig:transport-followup-outcomes});
46: \Cref{tab:transport-followup-outcomes} gives the numerical values.  All nine
47: paired 95\% intervals for comparator-minus-Hessian regret exclude zero.
48: These are pointwise intervals from 10,000 paired seed-bootstrap resamples per
49: comparison, without multiplicity adjustment.  They quantify evaluation-seed
50: variation conditional on the fixed teacher, design, and selected optimizer;
51: they do not include uncertainty from environment selection or tuning.
52: The comparisons are total-policy outcomes on matched exogenous streams, not
53: fixed-history interventions.  They establish neither a universal policy
54: ordering nor a causal attribution to the certificate alone.
55: 
56: For descriptive context, the online context-free mean-only benchmark has mean
57: regrets 185.26, 183.06, and 176.67 at $W=16,1,0.25$, respectively; the best fixed
58: action in hindsight has mean regrets 180.01, 177.97, and 171.84.  These means
59: use the same evaluation streams.  Hessian's sample means are close to the
60: context-free benchmark's, but no equivalence test was performed, and similar
61: regret does not imply matching actions or identical use of context.
62: \Cref{app:transport-followup} defines both benchmarks.
63: 
64: \begin{figure}[p]
65:   \centering
66:   \input{figures/transport_explanatory_outcomes.tex}
67:   \caption{Policy outcomes and paired comparisons in every prespecified
68:   condition.  Left: descriptive mean cumulative pseudo-regret at $T=1000$,
69:   without error bars.  Right: each comparator's regret minus Hessian's, with
70:   pointwise 95\% paired seed-bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples of
71:   50 seeds per condition.  Negative differences favor the comparator.
72:   The intervals condition on the fixed teacher, design and selected optimizer;
73:   they are not multiplicity-adjusted.  Each policy follows its own adaptive
74:   history on matched exogenous streams.  Changing $W$ changes the reward task
75:   as well as curvature, so the rows do not isolate an effect of drift.}
76:   \label{fig:transport-followup-outcomes}
77: \end{figure}
78: 
79: \paragraph{Realized drift, validity diagnostics, and vacuous bounds.}
80: The primary policy reaches endpoint distances above one in 16 of 50 seeds at
81: $W=0.25$, including 286 of 50,000 seed--round observations
82: (\Cref{tab:transport-followup-drift-bounds}).  These round counts describe
83: dependent observations, not additional independent replications.  Target
84: labels used to encode $W$ are not realized distances.
85: All 600 evaluation trajectories, including naive current, pass the recorded
86: simultaneous reference-confidence, method-optimism, and deterministic
87: diagnostics.  Each policy--condition cell has 50 successes out of 50, with an
88: exact 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval of approximately $[92.9\%,100\%]$.
89: This observation does not establish population coverage, validate the theorem,
90: or show that transport is necessary.  Float64 checks and converged quadrature
91: are numerical diagnostics, not verified enclosures.
92: 
93: The primary bounds are dominated by path inflation in all three conditions.
94: Every primary-policy bound exceeds the deterministic regret cap
95: $2T\min(1,\sqrt W)$, which is 2000, 2000, and 1000 for the three conditions.
96: The frozen policy's own reference-geometry bounds also exceed these caps in
97: all 150 of its trajectories.  Their mean right-hand sides are much smaller
98: than the primary bounds but remain vacuous.
99: \Cref{fig:transport-followup-bound-scale} makes their scale visible relative
100: to the cap; values above the cap provide no improvement over that deterministic
101: upper bound.  Removing the path term along
102: Hessian's histories would be an accounting decomposition, not the bound or
103: outcome of a frozen policy following different histories.  Base dominance
104: reported for the original near-linear grid does not describe this follow-up.
105:

131: \paragraph{Exploratory decision analysis.}
132: After observing these outcomes, we independently recomputed score diagnostics
133: from all 600 preserved trajectories.  On Hessian's own histories, its selected
134: action equals the current-width argmax on 99.382\%, 99.962\%, and 99.982\% of
135: rounds for $W=16,1,0.25$.  A stronger sufficient condition---the bonus gap
136: between the two largest widths exceeding the entire range of prediction
137: centers---holds on 97.104\%, 99.372\%, and 99.508\% of rounds.
138: These pooled fractions describe extensive width-dominated selection in the
139: visited states, not an adaptive causal mechanism or an independent-round test.
140: The per-seed mechanism table in \Cref{app:transport-followup} applies this same
141: Hessian score to all four behavior histories; it does not report width dominance
142: of each behavior policy's own score.  The appendix also compares alternative
143: score recommendations on fixed histories and checks early numerical ranking
144: sensitivity.  The fixed-history comparisons respect
145: \Cref{prop:reference-width-floor}: tightening a transport certificate does not
146: create additional statistical information or order policies' adaptive regret.
147: 
148: \paragraph{Exploratory tighter endpoint certificates.}
149: The relative-weight construction in \Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights} permits
150: uniform and category-specific endpoint comparisons without using the Hessian
151: path envelope.  We audit these comparisons on the same 600 recorded histories,
152: replaying representation updates with the recorded actions and rewards.
153: On primary histories, the category-specific outward factor gives mean
154: effective-width overheads of $0.28\%$--$12.68\%$ relative to the direct reference
155: width, versus $0.16\%$--$12.13\%$ for the dense endpoint factor across conditions
156: (\Cref{app:transport-followup}).  These are means of actionwise ratios, not
157: ratios of mean widths.  This analysis evaluates new scores
158: on existing states; it does not evaluate a new adaptive policy or demonstrate
159: an end-to-end computational advantage.  The relative certificate bounds an
160: endpoint comparison, not the original interpolated factor-path length, and
161: does not remove the historical and current approximation-error charges.
